viva.question: Is uniform convergence stronger or weaker than pointwise convergence?
viva.answer: Stronger — uniform convergence always implies pointwise convergence, never the reverse.
viva.why: The uniform definition requires one N to work for every x simultaneously, a strictly harder condition to satisfy than N depending on x.
viva.followUp: Does uniform convergence preserve differentiability of the limit?
viva.trap: Asking a student to 'prove' uniform convergence by checking only x=0 and x=1.

viva.question: Is every norm a metric?
viva.answer: Every norm induces a metric via d(x,y)=||x-y||, but not every metric arises from a norm.
viva.why: A metric space need not even be a vector space, so 'norm' doesn't always make sense, while distance always does.
viva.followUp: Give an example of a metric space that is not a normed space.
viva.trap: Assuming metric and norm are interchangeable concepts.

viva.question: Is Q, the rationals, complete under the usual metric?
viva.answer: No — Cauchy sequences of rationals can converge to irrational limits, which lie outside Q.
viva.why: Completeness requires the limit to lie IN the space; Q has 'holes' at every irrational number.
viva.followUp: What is the standard construction that completes Q?
viva.trap: Confusing 'bounded' with 'complete' — they are unrelated properties.

viva.question: Why does the Banach Fixed-Point Theorem require completeness?
viva.answer: The proof constructs the fixed point as the limit of a Cauchy sequence generated by iterating T; without completeness, that limit might not exist in the space.
viva.why: The whole argument is: contraction \Rightarrow the iterates form a Cauchy sequence \Rightarrow completeness gives a limit \Rightarrow that limit is the fixed point.
viva.followUp: Give an explicit contraction with no fixed point on an incomplete space.
viva.trap: Forgetting the theorem is an existence-AND-uniqueness statement, not just existence.
